summary: Turn every work task into a ticket with one owner, a status and a deadline, so everyone can see who is responsible for what and nothing slips through the cracks.
takeaways: Turn every task into a ticket with one clear owner
Track each ticket's status and deadline to catch delays early
Avoid lining dependent tasks up directly back-to-back
Route bug reports through tickets and reassign when needed

principles.principle: Turn every task into a ticket with one clear owner
principles.why: Tickets passed between team members through a server tool make it clear who is responsible for what, so status is easy to confirm and nothing slips through the cracks.
principles.how: Split one character into tickets for spec/doc, model and rig, animation, programming, VFX, SFX and balancing, each assigned to a leader or team member.
principles.anti_pattern: Work that lives only in conversation, with no owner or status.
principles.example: Making one game character: every production step becomes a ticket passed from team to team.
principles.quote: Manage those tasks, and make it crystal clear what needs to happen.

principles.principle: Give every ticket a status and a deadline a lead tracks
principles.why: Statuses like in progress, complete, on hold and rescinded make it easy to judge how things are going, and a leader tracking deadlines can head off delays.
principles.how: Require a status field and due date on each ticket and have leads review open tickets regularly.

principles.principle: Avoid lining up dependent tasks so directly back-to-back
principles.why: Downstream jobs depend on upstream ones (the animator can't work until the model is ready), and when work runs late the next person ends up starting early with whatever they have.
principles.how: Let dependent job types share a ticket and leave scheduling slack between upstream and downstream work.
principles.anti_pattern: Forcing downstream staff to start on unfinished upstream work.
principles.example: Animation waiting on the character model.
principles.quote: it's better to avoid lining tasks up so directly when possible.

principles.principle: Route bug reports through tickets via section leaders
principles.why: Testers confirm the bug and write the report inside the ticket, and the section leader distributes it to the right people; anyone can reassign it if it reached the wrong person or needs more eyes.
principles.how: Have testers file confirmed bugs as tickets, route them through leads, and allow free reassignment.
principles.example: Bug testers receiving, confirming and returning tickets.

summary: Go out of your way to praise players when they do something good—with crowds, allies, bonuses or celebratory effects—because items and progress are expected rewards that don't, on their own, tell players "well done."
takeaways: Praise players explicitly when they do something good
Items and progress are expected, so they aren't enough praise
Use crowds, allies, bonuses and confetti to celebrate plays
Match or heighten the player's feelings rather than stating the obvious

principles.principle: Praise good plays explicitly, beyond items and progress
principles.why: Games are meant to be fun; items and progress are expected by design and aren't there specifically to tell players they've done well.
principles.how: Add crowd cheers on big launches and KOs, or have allied characters praise the player based on feats like enemies defeated.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating item drops and progression as all the praise a player needs.
principles.example: Smash Bros. crowd cheers on launches, KOs and the victory screen; Dynasty Warriors commanders praise the player based on enemies defeated.
principles.quote: Games are meant to be fun, so it's important to praise players for doing something good.

principles.principle: Hand out bonuses generously, even when players stumble
principles.why: In Forza, whether you drive great or wreck your car, you still get some kind of bonus; these are praise too, and they're effective.
principles.how: Attach small named bonuses to many kinds of actions so acknowledgment keeps coming.
principles.example: Forza: bonuses for almost everything, including wrecking your car.
principles.quote: And they're effective, so don't hold back on including them in your game.

principles.principle: Add subtle crowd reactions to near-misses and close saves
principles.why: Smash's crowd gives a subtle "oh!" when you barely manage to grab a ledge, acknowledging the close call in the moment.
principles.how: Trigger quiet gasps on narrow escapes and louder cheers on big launches and KOs.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.: the crowd's "oh!" on a barely-made ledge grab.

principles.principle: Shape celebrations to heighten how the scoring player feels
principles.why: Smash Ultimate's KO confetti may seem odd for the player who erred, but it colorfully praises the one who scored; praise should match or heighten the player's feelings rather than being the most obvious expression.
principles.how: Add colorful celebratory effects to the scoring moment, aimed at the player who earned it.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate: confetti added to the KO explosion.
principles.quote: try not to express things in the most obvious fashion— instead, try to match how the player is feeling, or find a way to heighten those feelings.

summary: A platform (or a game) wins when strong graphics, sound, smooth performance, easy controls, a fair price and above all fun arrive together, and technical skill can pack far more game into the same tiny budget.
takeaways: Famicom won on graphics, sound, smoothness, controls, price and fun
Super Mario Bros. packed far more game into just 40 KB
Cartridge custom chips and expanded audio transformed the hardware
Japan's Famicom mania shaped the entire modern game industry

principles.principle: Pack more game into tight budgets through technical skill
principles.why: Mario Bros. was 24 KB and Super Mario Bros. 40 KB; that modest difference allowed for a lot more game thanks to shocking technical skill.
principles.how: When storage is limited, push craft and technique to deliver more content instead of assuming you need more space.
principles.example: Mario Bros. (24 KB) vs. Super Mario Bros. (40 KB).
principles.quote: The technical skill packed into these tiny ROMs was frankly shocking.

principles.principle: Deliver visuals, sound, smooth motion, easy controls and fun together
principles.why: The Famicom felt like a breath of fresh air because it combined gorgeous graphics, memorable sound, smooth processing, an easy controller and an affordable price, and best of all its games were fun.
principles.how: Check each of these fronts in your game, including smooth animation instead of sprites that jump between frames as they walk.
principles.example: Famicom vs. 1983 games with single-color blobs that jumped between frames.
principles.quote: Best of all, the games were fun.

principles.principle: Keep the original's game essence when moving to new hardware
principles.why: Part of the Famicom's wonder was playing the arcade hit Donkey Kong at home with more or less the same game essence.
principles.how: When porting or adapting a game, verify that the core play matches the original.
principles.example: Donkey Kong on Famicom.
principles.quote: You could even play the arcade hit Donkey Kong with more or less the same game essence.

summary: In competitive games, being defeated can relieve stress and defeating someone can create anxiety, so design deaths, restarts and kills so that both sides of the exchange are fun and players want another try.
takeaways: Competitive players can feel relief when defeated, anxiety after kills
Quick restarts sweep away disappointment before it sets in
A non-decisive kill shows a future where you're defeated
Make losing fun, not just dominating opponents

principles.principle: Keep restarts quick so defeat never has time to sting
principles.why: Whether the clock keeps running or a rematch begins, relatively quick restarts keep players pushing forward with no time to feel upset.
principles.how: Minimize respawn and rematch delays and drop players straight back into play.
principles.anti_pattern: Long post-death waits that let disappointment set in.
principles.quote: as long as restart times are relatively quick, you can keep pushing forward— you won't have time to feel upset.

principles.principle: Design being defeated to be fun, not only defeating others
principles.why: A study found competitive FPS players feel relief when defeated; when the fun of both defeating and being defeated clicks, there's no better entertainment.
principles.how: Plan how each death motivates a retry, aiming for the reaction "I'll get you next time!"
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming competitive fun is only the joy of dominating opponents.
principles.example: Overseas study of competitive first-person shooter players.
principles.quote: Remember, competitive games aren't only about the joy of dominating your opponent.

principles.principle: Account for the tension a non-decisive kill creates
principles.why: The real objective is to win; if a kill doesn't settle the match it's too soon to relax, and it hints that you could be the next one defeated.
principles.how: When tuning match flow, expect mid-match kills to raise the scorer's tension rather than relieve it.
principles.quote: In a way, defeating an opponent shows you a potential future where you're the one defeated.

summary: To keep routine creative output going for years, keep it light: play to strengths you already use, cap the time it takes, and drop the sense of obligation so you enjoy the work instead of feeling beholden to it.
takeaways: Approach routine work loosely, not out of obligation
Keep recurring tasks short; each column took about an hour
Play to strengths you already use daily
Ignore pressure and publish what you think is good

principles.principle: Approach routine work loosely, not out of obligation
principles.why: Working out of obligation or "for the sake of the industry" takes a major toll; staying looser let him keep a column going for 18 years and 9 months.
principles.how: Shrug off pressure and duty, and put out what you think is good without overthinking it.
principles.anti_pattern: Writing because you have to or because many people are reading.
principles.example: Weekly Famitsu column: 640 articles.
principles.quote: You have to enjoy it, not feel beholden to it.

principles.principle: Keep recurring deliverables small in time investment
principles.why: He typically finished each column in about an hour, a reasonable investment that stayed sustainable even through busy dev periods and all-nighters.
principles.how: Time-box recurring output to a short, fixed slot.
principles.example: Weekly Famitsu column.
principles.quote: When writing the columns, I typically finished in about an hour.

principles.principle: Choose recurring output that uses strengths you already exercise
principles.why: As a director, conveying ideas isn't a chore for him, it's what he does, so writing a column came naturally.
principles.how: Pick side projects that line up with the skills your main job already trains.
principles.quote: Being a director, I don't find conveying ideas to be too much of a chore.

summary: Study shipped stages up close as art reference: Smash Bros. Ultimate recreated the worlds of dozens of games in one title while holding 60 fps with eight fighters on-screen, which left the stage team little performance leeway.
takeaways: Ultimate has around 115 base stages from many games
Eight fighters at 60 fps on Switch left little leeway
Study close-up stage views as environment art reference

principles.principle: Budget stage art for the worst-case load at target frame rate
principles.why: Ultimate's stages had to run on Switch with eight fighters on-screen at 60 fps, which really didn't leave much leeway.
principles.how: Profile each stage with the maximum number of characters active and keep its art within that budget.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Ultimate's roughly 115 base stages.
principles.quote: Making them work on Nintendo Switch with eight fighters on-screen at 60 frames per second really didn't give us much leeway.

principles.principle: Study shipped stages up close as environment art reference
principles.why: He presented close-up views of the Stage team's work as great reference for aspiring game artists.
principles.how: Review finished game environments from close camera views to learn how each recreated world is built.
principles.example: Close-ups of 33 Ultimate stages, from Jungle Japes to Hollow Bastion.
principles.quote: it should prove great reference for any aspiring game artists.

summary: Treat hard limits as design fuel: reuse and mirror art to fit tiny memory, fake expensive systems with hand-placed patterns when processing is scarce, and visualize the design concretely early so the team can move forward with confidence.
takeaways: Mirror, flip and share sprite parts to stretch tiny ROM
Make bosses big so beginners' slightly off-target attacks hit
Hand-placed enemy paths replaced costly terrain collision on Game Boy
Smash's knockback rules already existed in his 1990 Kirby doc
Visualize designs early so the team moves forward confidently

principles.principle: Build similar characters from shared, flipped sprite parts
principles.why: Kirby was largely designed for 512 kilobits (64 KB), so Waddle Dee and Waddle Doo share a back half: two characters in the ROM space of 1.5.
principles.how: Mirror one image to animate (Gordo), reuse parts across variants (Kracko's eye for Kracko Jr.), and cap limb frames (Poppy Bros. Sr.: three leg and two head patterns).
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land: Waddle Dee/Waddle Doo, Gordo, Kracko, and the flip-friendly "M" on the Maxim Tomato.
principles.quote: To be blunt, I wanted to make two characters using the ROM space of only 1.5.

principles.principle: Make bosses big so newcomers' near-miss attacks still connect
principles.why: Kirby was made for newcomers, so even slightly off-target attacks should still hit; ROM limits led to Whispy Woods being one mirrored piece placed three times on the background.
principles.how: In beginner-focused games, give bosses large bodies, building them from background art if the sprite budget is tight.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land: Whispy Woods.
principles.quote: Kirby was a game made for newcomers, so even attacks that are slightly off-target should still hit.

principles.principle: Fake costly systems with hand-authored patterns when processing is scarce
principles.why: Kirby's enemies had no terrain collision; their movement was authored to match the background, which was wasteful to make but light on processing, invaluable on Game Boy, and kept Cappy bouncy.
principles.how: Script fixed enemy paths that mimic falls, ledges and water slowdown instead of running per-frame collision checks.
principles.example: Kirby's Dream Land: Coner, Waddle Dee and Cappy movement patterns.
principles.quote: Mainly, it was light on processing power. This was an invaluable benefit when working with the Game Boy.

principles.principle: Visualize the design concretely early so the team proceeds confidently
principles.why: It's easier for the team to move forward confidently with concrete visuals.
principles.how: Mock up characters at their intended size and map full movesets before full production; Kirby Super Star's Fighter moveset and Final Cutter combo survived from such early sketches.
principles.example: Kirby Super Star prototypes made in the Famicom dev tool.
principles.quote: Since the beginning, it's been my style with Kirby to visualize the design as clearly as possible in the early stages of the project.

summary: Make your title, box art, screenshots and trailers show what your game actually feels like, because a misleading image misses the players who would love it and disappoints the ones it fools.
takeaways: Marketing images must match how the game actually feels
Misleading packaging misses real fans and disappoints misled buyers
Pick titles that abbreviate memorably, like "Smash"
Subvert expectations only while capturing the game's heart

principles.principle: Make every marketing image match how the game actually feels
principles.why: If the game's image and reality don't match, you fail to reach the people it would resonate with and disappoint those misled into buying it.
principles.how: Check the title, box art, screenshots and trailers against actual play and fix anything that sets the wrong expectation.
principles.anti_pattern: Painting a misleading picture just to surprise players, like a banana that tastes like an apple.
principles.quote: No matter how much you want to catch your players by surprise, don't paint a picture that doesn't represent your game!

principles.principle: Choose a title that abbreviates into something memorable
principles.why: Super Smash Bros. can become just "Smash," which may help people remember it more easily.
principles.how: While naming, list the short forms players will likely use and prefer names that shorten well.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. → "Smash."

principles.principle: Subvert expectations only if it still captures the game's heart
principles.why: Kirby Super Star's simple wooden-box cover seemed unrelated to the vibrant game but got straight to the heart of it; still, showing the game for what it is works better.
principles.how: Use indirect or surprising packaging sparingly, and make sure it conveys the core feeling of the game.
principles.example: Kirby Super Star (Japan): wooden-box cover proposed by Shigesato Itoi.
principles.quote: There's a time and place for subverting expectations, but the more effective strategy is to show your game for what it truly is.

summary: Decide action by action whether a character can fall off a ledge, letting momentum-heavy rushes go over while short steps and dodges stop at the edge, so players never feel their input was canceled or that they slid off by accident.
takeaways: Decide ledge-falling per action, not with one global rule
Forward-stepping actions that fall off feel like canceled inputs
Account for momentum and move phase near ledges
Playtest ledge behavior for feel

principles.principle: Decide ledge-falling per action instead of one global rule
principles.why: Characters that always fall hurt many old games; Sakurai says letting some actions fall and others not is the way to do it.
principles.how: Make forward dodges stop at edges while forward-rushing attacks carry over.
principles.anti_pattern: Making characters fall off ledges regardless of conditions.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.: Fox Illusion stops at the ledge; Falcon Kick goes straight over.
principles.quote: Falling off ledges isn't as straightforward as it seems.

principles.principle: Never let small forward nudges drop players off ledges
principles.why: If an action that nudges the character forward drops them off the ledge, it feels like their input was canceled.
principles.how: Keep stepping attacks and similar small forward motions on the platform.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting the slight forward motion of an attack carry the player over the edge.
principles.quote: If you let a player fall off a ledge the moment they're nudged forward by an action, it may make them feel like their input was canceled—which isn't great.

principles.principle: Gate ledge falls by momentum and move phase
principles.why: Without accounting for momentum, it's too easy to go flying off the stage.
principles.how: Make rushes stop at the ledge near the end of the move (Falcon Kick, Drill Rush) and set a speed threshold for rolling moves like Egg Roll.
principles.anti_pattern: Ignoring momentum near edges.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.: Falcon Kick, Drill Rush, Yoshi's Egg Roll speed parameters.

principles.principle: Help walking players at edges with push-to-fall or steering
principles.why: Falling off ledges isn't straightforward; requiring a push against the ledge, or adjusting movement direction when the ledge is nearly parallel to it, are effective techniques.
principles.how: Require continued input toward the edge before falling, or bend movement along near-parallel ledges; some games even auto-jump at ledges.

summary: Use screen shake to sell big impacts—with a distinct pattern per impact size, scaled to camera distance and field of view, decaying with some randomness—but never so much that the screen becomes hard to read.
takeaways: Screen shake sells big impacts, but don't overdo it
Use distinct shake patterns per size, not scaled copies
Scale shake to camera distance and field of view
Start strong, decay gradually, add some randomness

principles.principle: Use distinct shake patterns per impact size, not scaled copies
principles.why: Smash's large, medium and small shakes aren't scaled versions of one shake but different patterns: small is vertical only, medium adds horizontal, large shakes more.
principles.how: Author 3–4 shake presets with different axis behavior and map them to impact strength.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. large/medium/small/extra-small shakes.
principles.quote: Large, medium, and small aren't just scaled versions of the same shake, but actually use different patterns entirely.

principles.principle: Scale shake to camera distance and field of view
principles.why: Adjusting shake by camera distance keeps it from feeling off, and a tight field of view makes the usual shake feel really big.
principles.how: Multiply shake amplitude by a camera-distance/FOV factor and retune scenes with unusual FOV.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.: Flat Zone's tighter field of view needed reduced shake.
principles.quote: We change the size of the screen shake based on the distance of the camera.

principles.principle: Shake the camera's look-at point too, not just the camera
principles.why: With 3D camera shake, distant objects barely move; if a far-off center point moves too subtly, it won't look like much is happening.
principles.how: Sync the look-at point's shake with the camera, or shake it even more than the camera itself.
principles.anti_pattern: Moving a distant center point so subtly that the shake doesn't read.

principles.principle: Start shakes strong and decay them with some randomness
principles.why: A shake that starts strong, gradually subsides and isn't a clean whirlpool pattern feels nicer; too much shake makes the screen hard to see.
principles.how: Use a decaying envelope with a slightly randomized path, and cap amplitude so the screen stays readable.
principles.anti_pattern: Shaking so much that the screen becomes difficult to see.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. shake implementation.
principles.quote: Even a tiny amount of shake can give attacks a drastically different impact.

summary: Make sure every button press gets some reaction: map confirm to several buttons, double up functions, and let presses during cutscenes bring up a skip prompt, because players press buttons when they want something from the game.
takeaways: Every button press should get some reaction
Map menu confirm to more than one button
Redundant button functions beat dead buttons
Let button presses in cutscenes bring up a skip prompt

principles.principle: Give every button press some reaction
principles.why: Information from the player's hands is vital, and an action with no reaction feels lacking; games are all about actions and reactions.
principles.how: Audit each game state for dead buttons and give them a redundant function or at least visible feedback.
principles.anti_pattern: Buttons that do nothing when pressed.
principles.quote: Players press buttons because they want something from the game.

principles.principle: Map menu confirm to more than one button
principles.why: Everyone has their own way of playing, and if L also works as confirm, players can even play one-handed; feeling around for buttons beats unresponsive controls.
principles.how: Accept the main confirm button plus a shoulder button such as L in menus and other UI.
principles.example: Using L as an extra confirm/action button.
principles.quote: For menus and other UI bits, I'd say it's better to have more than one button act as a confirm button.

principles.principle: Let button presses during cutscenes bring up a skip prompt
principles.why: Players press buttons because they want something from the game, so cutscenes especially should respond.
principles.how: On any button press during a cutscene, show a prompt that allows skipping.
principles.anti_pattern: Cutscenes that ignore button presses entirely.

principles.principle: Make press feedback unambiguous
principles.why: Ambiguous responses that don't clearly show whether a button was pressed undermine the action-reaction loop.
principles.how: Give each accepted press a distinct sound, highlight or animation.
principles.anti_pattern: Feedback so subtle players can't tell if their press registered.
principles.quote: It's also good to avoid ambiguous responses that don't clearly show whether a button was pressed.

summary: Don't scale enemy strength in lockstep with the player's growth; shape progression like a mountain trail with peaks (bosses that demand a strategy and pay off) and flat stretches (quiet areas, places to rack up gains), so advancing feels like adventure rather than work.
takeaways: Don't keep enemy strength proportional to player strength
Shape progression like a trail with peaks and valleys
Bosses should demand strategy and reward success
Add empty areas and farming spots as breathers
Enemy scaling with the player removes the incentive to get ahead

principles.principle: Don't scale enemy strength in direct proportion to player growth
principles.why: A steady incline the whole way is a chore, especially with unchanging scenery or only periodic rest stops: it's just work.
principles.how: Plot player vs. enemy strength and reshape it into peaks of challenge and flat stretches.
principles.anti_pattern: A straight diagonal line of player and enemy strength rising together.
principles.example: Mountain-climbing analogy.
principles.quote: My point is, it's not a good idea to keep player and enemy strength in direct proportion.

principles.principle: Make bosses demand a strategy, then reward pulling it off
principles.why: Bosses are the challenge peaks, and they shouldn't just be stronger versions of regular enemies.
principles.how: Design each boss so players must form a strategy, and give a nice reward once they succeed.
principles.anti_pattern: Bosses that are just beefed-up regular enemies.
principles.quote: placing a boss should force the player to form a strategy, and once they're able to pull it off, they should get a nice reward for their trouble.

principles.principle: Add flat stretches: empty areas and spots to rack up gains
principles.why: Flatter areas, like an unexpectedly empty space or a spot to rack up gains, make exploration more fun.
principles.how: Place quiet, enemy-free zones amid dense areas and include farming spots.
principles.quote: Measures like these are what make game exploration even more fun.

principles.principle: Avoid level-scaling enemies alongside the player
principles.why: If enemies get stronger along with the player, you remove any incentive for getting ahead.
principles.how: In open, multi-direction games, find balancing that keeps growth rewarding and leaves room for interesting strategies.
principles.anti_pattern: Enemies that always scale to the player's level.
principles.quote: If you include a system where enemies get stronger along with the player, you'll remove any incentive for getting ahead.

summary: Develop an eye for cool poses by physically handling an action figure—breaking symmetry and straight lines, angling the head and limbs, and shifting the balance off-center until it looks good—because if the fundamental pose is off, no finishing touch will save it.
takeaways: Practice posing with a physical action figure
Break symmetry; use S-curves and angled heads and limbs
Keep arms near the torso, wrists bent, feet at varied depths
A bad fundamental pose ruins even polished artwork

principles.principle: Practice posing with a physical action figure
principles.why: Having a physical object to reference teaches a great deal about what makes a pose cool and which angle works best.
principles.how: Keep a posable figure at hand, pose it and zoom it around (bundodo) to train your eye.
principles.example: Pit figma figure.
principles.quote: If you want to develop an eye for posing, there's no better way than to toy with a physical figure

principles.principle: Break symmetry and straight lines to make poses dynamic
principles.why: A figure stood up normally isn't terribly exciting; asymmetry and varied lines make it dashing.
principles.how: Avoid left-right symmetry and straight-on facing, lower the chin, tilt the head off right angles, and give torso, hips and legs different lines (an S curve).
principles.anti_pattern: Symmetrical, front-facing standing poses.
principles.example: Pit figma: default vs. adjusted standing pose.

principles.principle: Shape arms, wrists and feet with the silhouette in mind
principles.why: Small limb details change how cool a pose reads, even on a stationary figure.
principles.how: Set arms at different bent angles close to the torso, bend wrists slightly forward, shift the center of gravity off-middle, and angle feet outward at different camera depths.
principles.anti_pattern: Arms far from the torso and wrists as straight extensions of the arms.

principles.principle: Fix the fundamental pose before finishing touches
principles.why: Smash Bros. artwork is polished down to the finishing touches, but it all comes down to posing.
principles.how: Approve the base pose first, then judge by eye rather than formula before polishing.
principles.anti_pattern: Polishing art whose base pose is off.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. official artwork.
principles.quote: If the fundamental pose is off, it just won't look right.

summary: Voice sessions are short but their results live in the game forever, so script every vocalization, bring reference audio, keep in-battle lines short and non-competing, and budget plenty of editing time afterward.
takeaways: One fighter's voice recording takes about one hour
Script every grunt, or it won't be recorded
Keep battle lines short so chatter doesn't break immersion
Expect heavy voice editing after recording sessions
games: Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS / Wii U

principles.principle: Script every vocalization, down to each grunt
principles.why: Sessions are short (about an hour per Smash fighter), and anything not in the script won't get recorded.
principles.how: List basics (attacks, jumps, damage reactions) and unique lines (special moves, Final Smashes, reveal dialogue), plus reference audio from the original game.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving small grunts and reactions out of the script.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. voice scripts.
principles.quote: Every “ha" or “hmph” needs to be on there in order to get recorded.

principles.principle: Keep in-battle voice lines short and sparse
principles.why: Longer lines or excessive chatter in battle draw too much attention and break player immersion.
principles.how: Cap combat lines to short barks and limit how often they trigger.
principles.anti_pattern: Long lines and constant chatter during gameplay.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. fighter voices.
principles.quote: Longer lines or excessive chatter in battle can draw too much attention and break player immersion.

principles.principle: Plan how voices overlap so they don't compete
principles.why: It's not good to have voices competing with each other, especially loud, feral-sounding ones.
principles.how: Test simultaneous vocalizations from multiple characters and adjust timing or volume where they clash.
principles.anti_pattern: Voices stacking and fighting for attention.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.: Bowser and Donkey Kong.

principles.principle: Budget heavy editing time after recording
principles.why: Surprisingly, it's after recording that things really get busy, as voices are edited over and over to suit the game.
principles.how: Schedule post-session editing as a major task, not an afterthought.
principles.quote: Surprisingly, it's after the recording that things really get busy, as voices get edited over and over to make them suitable for the game.

summary: Build a sequel's concept around what its platform and audience need—for Brawl, online play and a single-player mode of appropriate length—while slowing the controls for casual players and giving every character individuality.
takeaways: Brawl's concept pillars: online support and a substantial single-player mode
Slower speed and lower input density suited casual Wii players
Final Smashes gave every fighter individuality instead of a generic item
Subspace Emissary needed separate movement parameters per fighter

principles.principle: Slow the pace and input density for casual audiences
principles.why: Melee's speed was great for top players but too harsh on new players, even causing tendinitis; the Wii targeted casual players, sideways Wii Remotes, and laggy online where dense inputs make frame skips stand out.
principles.how: Lower game speed and the input density required, and tune toward casual play when the platform or audience calls for it.
principles.anti_pattern: Keeping a hardcore, high-speed control scheme for a casual audience.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Melee → Brawl.
principles.quote: So, we kept the game's speed a little slower. And we tuned it more toward casual gameplay.

principles.principle: Tune separate movement parameters for each very different mode
principles.why: Dropping fighters into the Subspace Emissary with their Versus Mode specs didn't work.
principles.how: Give characters a separate jump/movement parameter set per mode, and budget time to tune both sets.
principles.anti_pattern: Reusing one mode's specs unchanged in a very different mode.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl: Subspace Emissary parameters.
principles.quote: It didn't work just dropping fighters in with their specs from Versus Mode, so we made all sorts of adjustments.

principles.principle: Make power features unique per character to build individuality
principles.why: A powerful attack could have been a simple item, but giving everyone a unique Final Smash boosted each character's individuality.
principles.how: When a feature could be generic, consider a per-character version that showcases each one.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl: Final Smashes.
principles.quote: since we wanted to really boost the individuality of each character, everyone got their own unique move.

principles.principle: Match synchronous online players within the same local region
principles.why: Smash needs fully synchronous communication, unlike asynchronous games like Mario Kart, so lag makes it choppy unless players are close.
principles.how: For real-time synchronous games, matchmake within the same region rather than just the same country.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros. Brawl online vs. Mario Kart.
principles.quote: it works best sticking to not just your own country, but even your own local region within it.

summary: In proposals and design docs, commit to the one spec you think is best instead of listing alternatives, and course-correct as a team if problems come up.
takeaways: Drop Plan B; commit to the best spec
Start ideal, then course-correct for cost-effectiveness
Resolve problems as a team after proposing
The proposal is the game's skeleton; don't twist it

principles.principle: Commit to one spec in proposals; drop Plan B
principles.why: Writing "or we could do this" leaves the decision to someone else; standing by one idea shows you've really thought it through and builds experience.
principles.how: Look at the whole picture, pick the method you think works best, and cut hypotheticals and secondary ideas from the proposal.
principles.anti_pattern: Leaving both doors open in a proposal.
principles.quote: But with proposals in particular, you're better off ditching Plan B entirely.

principles.principle: Start from the ideal spec, then course-correct for cost
principles.why: Beginning with the ideal and adjusting afterward to maximize cost-effectiveness is more than good enough.
principles.how: Write the ideal version first and trim only when concrete problems surface.
principles.anti_pattern: Twisting the proposal out of shape up front for dev efficiency.
principles.quote: There should always be an ideal spec to start, and from there you can course-correct to maximize cost effectiveness.

principles.principle: Resolve spec problems together with the team after proposing
principles.why: The proposal-writer should start with the ideal, field plenty of suggestions with an open mind, and address problems as a team, even if that ends at Plan B.
principles.how: Circulate the proposal, gather team feedback, and revisit alternatives only when real problems arise.
principles.quote: If problems arise, you can then address them as a team.

summary: Any game can be canceled, usually when remaining costs outweigh expected revenue, so everyone on the team should understand what it takes to actually finish the game instead of assuming it will ship once they've done their own tasks.
takeaways: Cancellations weigh remaining costs against expected revenue
Costs peak late: testing, marketing, largest headcount
Finishing tasks alone doesn't guarantee a finished game
Everyone should know what's needed to ship

principles.principle: Make everyone aware of what it takes to finish the game
principles.why: The more each team member knows what's needed to finish, the better the odds of seeing it through; finishing assignments alone doesn't guarantee a finished product.
principles.how: Share a visible picture of everything remaining to ship, not just per-person task lists, and work through it together.
principles.anti_pattern: Assuming the game will ship just because everyone completes their assigned tasks.
principles.quote: At the very least, you shouldn't assume that you'll end up with a finished product just because everyone completes what they're assigned.

principles.principle: Cut a doomed project before the costly final stretch
principles.why: Costs are highest toward the end (testing, marketing, the most people), and cancellation is about cutting losses.
principles.how: Re-weigh remaining development cost against realistic expected revenue before scaling up for the end of the cycle.
principles.anti_pattern: Pushing a project you don't believe in into its most expensive phase.
principles.quote: Cancellation is about cutting your losses, so if you don't think you can make it, it's best to get out while you still can.

summary: Use fonts, UI frames, icons, colors and decoration to establish your game's world and target audience while keeping text legible, because the same content can feel adult, cute, horror or historical just by changing its presentation.
takeaways: Fonts and UI can retarget the same game's audience
Changing fonts conveys a world more cheaply than new art
Theme frames, icons, colors and decorations too
Stay legible while designing immersive UI

principles.principle: Use font and UI style to set the world and audience
principles.why: Two games with the same essence and content can target different audiences just by tweaking the UI or font, which is much easier than redesigning characters or environments.
principles.how: Mock up one menu in several styles (slick, cute, horror, flashy, digital, regional) and pick the one that fits your world.
principles.anti_pattern: Treating menus as neutral afterthoughts.
principles.example: Same options screen shown in many styles.
principles.quote: Fonts and UI are both a part of a game's worldbuilding. You might even say they're the package that the world is wrapped in.

principles.principle: Keep themed UI legible
principles.why: You want to maintain legibility while proactively designing immersive visuals.
principles.how: Check every themed font and frame for readability at actual screen size before locking it.
principles.anti_pattern: Styling text so heavily it can't be read.
principles.quote: You want to maintain legibility, all while proactively designing immersive visuals.

principles.principle: Theme frames, icons, colors and decorations, not just fonts
principles.why: Backgrounds, frames, icons, color choices and decorations all lend the world atmosphere.
principles.how: Style every menu element to match the setting, and choose fonts deliberately even in minimalist designs.

summary: Choose your target audience from a top-down view of the market rather than your own tastes, remembering that tastes branch apart with age, so the broadest market is the "trunk" of younger players while a niche "branch" can still breed devoted fans.
takeaways: Target from a top-down market view, not personal taste
Tastes branch with age; young players form the broad trunk
Niche branches can create devoted fans
Era-appropriate successors pass enthusiasm to new generations

principles.principle: Pick your target from a top-down market view, not taste
principles.why: Players' styles have diversified widely, so relying on your own likes and dislikes misreads the market.
principles.how: Map current player segments and deliberately choose which one your game serves.
principles.anti_pattern: Choosing a target audience from personal preference alone.
principles.quote: The more aware you are of the market, the better you'll be able to target it— and that's really the main point here.

principles.principle: For broad hits, aim at the shared tastes of young players
principles.why: Values branch apart as people age, so the market is broadest at the trunk, before everyone finds their own branch; orthodox games and series fit values many players hold dear.
principles.how: Use orthodox, broadly appealing design and create era-appropriate successors so enthusiasm passes to the next generation.
principles.example: Nintendo's top sellers being hits with younger generations.
principles.quote: In a world full of diverse tastes, the market is broadest at the stage before everyone finds their own branch.

principles.principle: Target a niche branch deliberately for devoted fans
principles.why: Aiming a game directly at one branch might make its players really fall in love with it, so not every game has to target the trunk.
principles.how: If you go niche, commit to that branch's values instead of hedging toward everyone.

summary: Write game stories around play—start with gameplay, brief players as they go, keep the protagonist's perspective, and don't let story undo the player's wins or strip their party—breaking these rules only on purpose.
takeaways: Start with gameplay, not story
Brief players during play instead of before missions
Don't let cutscenes negate the player's victories
Avoid removing party members and their valuable items
Break these rules only deliberately, for memorability

principles.principle: Start with gameplay, not story; save details for later
principles.why: Players nowadays won't always latch onto a story, and long cutscenes keep action players from playing.
principles.how: Skip long prologue exposition, put players in control immediately, and brief them while they play.
principles.anti_pattern: Long-winded background explanations in the prologue.
principles.example: Kid Icarus: Uprising: Pit runs through a door and gameplay begins; briefings happen during play.
principles.quote: Start with gameplay, not with story.

principles.principle: Never let a cutscene negate a victory the player earned
principles.why: Winning a battle only to lose in the following cutscene is frustrating; negating achievements through story causes real stress.
principles.how: Keep the protagonist victorious in fights the player wins, and don't stage a story loss right after a player win.
principles.anti_pattern: Story beats that undo the player's victories.
principles.quote: Negating the player's achievements through story writing can cause some real stress.

principles.principle: Don't remove party members the player relies on
principles.why: Killing off or removing comrades works in other media, but in games it can throw off party balance or cost players valuable items.
principles.how: If a companion must leave, protect party balance and the items the player invested, or reconsider the beat.
principles.anti_pattern: Losing party members and their gear to a story event.

principles.principle: Tell the story from the protagonist's perspective
principles.why: Game stories generally unfold from the main character's view; lengthy backstory about comrades or villains, common in comics, often doesn't fit games.
principles.how: Trim side-character exposition and keep story beats tied to what the player character experiences.
principles.anti_pattern: Long backstory digressions about allies and villains.
principles.quote: The story generally unfolds from the main character's perspective.

summary: Give instructions and feedback to every relevant team member at once in a shared session, instead of relaying through one person, because it costs some meeting time but greatly improves understanding and visibility.
takeaways: Give feedback to all involved disciplines at once
Relayed instructions can come back as the opposite
Seeing others' feedback helps everyone learn and grow
Keep group sessions speedy to justify the meeting time
games: Super Smash Bros. for Nintendo 3DS / Wii U

principles.principle: Give feedback to every involved discipline at the same time
principles.why: On Kid Icarus: Uprising, instructions relayed through a planner to programmers sometimes came back as the polar opposite of what he wanted.
principles.how: Have planners, programmers, modelers, animators, VFX, sound and their leads all attend feedback sessions, with the build on a big monitor and a mic.
principles.anti_pattern: Relaying a director's intent through a chain of people.
principles.example: Super Smash Bros.: Inkling's special-move spec supervision.
principles.quote: Namely, whenever I gave instructions or feedback, all relevant team members were required to attend and listen.

principles.principle: Let people see the feedback others receive
principles.why: When team members see everyone's feedback, not just their own, they all learn and grow, and visibility improves on large projects.
principles.how: Hold group review sessions per discipline and let anyone sit in on feedback, even from other teams.
principles.example: Group review sessions for fighter modelers, artists, stage modelers and animators.
principles.quote: By having team members see the feedback everyone was getting—not just their own— they could all learn and grow.

principles.principle: Keep group feedback sessions speedy
principles.why: Extra meetings can look wasteful, and the system only works if they stay quick.
principles.how: Run tight sessions: show the screen, explain with a mic, then take questions at the end.
principles.anti_pattern: Letting large group meetings drag on.
principles.quote: It does require you to keep those meetings speedy for it to work, but I really do recommend it.
